claims.text: Applying a rare-earth oxide coating can improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The intervention is the application of a rare-earth oxide coating.
The proposed treatment applies to refractory high-entropy alloys in an as-cast or wrought state.
The coating promotes formation of a protective oxide scale.
The rare-earth oxide coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion reduces oxide-scale formation.
Reduced oxide-scale formation improves oxidation resistance.
Relative to an untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, the coated alloy will exhibit reduced oxidation kinetics.
Relative to an untreated refractory high-entropy alloy, the coated alloy will have an increased lifespan.
The proposed operating boundary is 800–1200°C in air for exposures of up to 100 hours.
A representative test condition is 1000°C in air.
Oxidation resistance can be compared using weight gain and oxide-scale thickness.
SEM or TEM can be used to assess the post-exposure microstructure.
The hypothesis is falsified if the coated alloy shows no significant improvement in oxidation resistance relative to the uncoated control.
The exact mechanism by which the coating affects oxidation resistance is not fully understood.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator says the coating causes formation of a protective oxide scale, whereas the mechanism says it improves resistance by reducing oxide-scale formation. The hypothesis does not distinguish a thin protective scale from detrimental oxide growth, so these statements conflict as written.
